verses.1: Al-Mizan treats tabb and tabāb—whether called loss, perpetual loss, failure, or deprivation of good—as near-equivalent expressions. “The hands” stand for the acts and efforts by which a person pursues aims: their tabāb means those efforts are void and fruitless, while tabba for the person means losing the soul by deprivation of eternal happiness, an everlasting ruin. The verse may be an imprecation against Abū Lahab’s attempts to extinguish prophethood or a statement of God’s judgment. It concerns the Prophet’s uncle, his persistent verbal and practical persecutor, whose “May you perish” at the first call to his relatives is returned by the sūrah. Of several proposed explanations of his name, Al-Mizan prefers the derogatory kunyah: “Father of Flame” marks him as a hellish man and anticipates the blazing fire of (111:3).
verses.2: Al-Mizan says that neither Abū Lahab’s wealth nor what he earned can avert the ruin of his hands and soul, whether that ruin is decreed or imprecated. The second mā may mean either what his deeds acquired—their consequences—or his very acquisition, namely his deeds.
verses.3:
Al-Mizan explains yaṣlá as entering the eternal fire of hell, whose indefinite description stresses its vastness and horror. The conjunction makes Abū Lahab’s wife enter it with him. Ḥammālat al-ḥaṭab is grammatically accusative as the object of an implied rebuke—“I condemn the firewood carrier”—though it has also been read as a circumstantial qualifier; masad is rope of twisted fibers. Because she used to cast thorny branches and similar harms in the Prophet’s path, the apparent sense is that she will be punished in hell in that same form, carrying firewood with such a rope around her neck.

Majmaʿ al-bayān asks whether the prophecy still left Abū Lahab obliged and able to believe, and answers that the threats were conditional on his persisting in unbelief. Al-Mizan says the question rests on a false premise: God’s irrevocable decree concerning voluntary acts does not abolish choice. When He wills a voluntary act, He wills it to occur through the agent’s volition; making the agent involuntary would not fulfill that will. Thus Abū Lahab could have believed and escaped the fire, but freely did not, and entry into hell was irrevocably decreed on account of that voluntary denial. The same principle applies to forecasts of Quraysh’s disbelief in (2:6) and (36:7), and to the sealing of hearts.
